newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia August employment data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia August employment data.

text.p: Australian employment rose 37,900 in August, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said. The unemployment rate was 8.8 percent.
Economists' median expectations had centred on a 11,000 employment rise and an 8.5 percent unemployment rate.
At the same time, retiring RBA governor Bernie Fraser and his replacement Ian Macfarlane are currently testifying to a parliamentray banking committee.
The following is a selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data.
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"It (employment) was obviously higher than expected as a result of the 10,000 Census workers in that 37,900 rise. If you take those off it is a medium rise in employment and may at the margins make it a little less likely the RBA will cut rates again if this employment growth is maintained for the rest of the year. Unemployment was attributable to participation and therefore I'd be cautious. But we still think there could be another rate cut."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"It's a bit baffling. There is very strong employment growth and a higher unemployment rate. My disposition is always to place more importance on the unemployment rate, so you can't claim that this is a strong report."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, STATE BANK OF NSW:

"It's always encouraging when jobs are created. The picture does get messed up by the census collectors. On balance you'd say, well the economy isn't falling over, it's continuing along at reasonable growth....If wages are under control, inflation is low and the unemployment rate is high, a strong case can be made for lower interest rates this year.
DAVID de GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"Obviously, it (employment) was right at the top end or over the top end of market expectations. The way the reserve bank will look at this figure is that it is bloated by the 10,000 Census collectors. These monthly figures are volatile. The full-time growth is a better indicator of the underlying trend. The growth is consistent with the pattern of the last three months, nothing has changed very much. It is always soft in the September quarter and we still believe the door is ajar for another easing."
GRANT BAILEY, CHIEF ECONOMIST CITIBANK AUSTRALIA

"They were a bit of a mixed bag. If they (the RBA) still have a bias towards easing, it doesn't move them any further towards an easing, and it doesn't move them away from that either. It really confirms what they already know and they don't get carried away by one month's figures unless it shows them way out of expectations, and this isn't it."
ALAN OSTER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"There's a bit of volatility in these numbers. The employment numbers were a little bit stronger (than the bank's forecast), but in trend terms they are still around 10,000, 12,000 to 13,000 (jobs per month increase). We expected that the employment situation would start to improve from the middle of the year, which seems to be happening now." Oster said there were no monetary policy implications from these monthly figures. "I think the market is still weak...."
BILL EVANS, GENERAL MANAGER ECONOMICS, WESTPAC BANK:

"It's obviously a bit stronger in total than the market was expecting..., but the full-time (job) numbers are not increasing enough to have any sort of an impact on unemployment. We need to see them moving faster." He said the figures showed the labour market was still weak and did not alter the bank's forecast for another near-term cut in official interest rates. "The government would be disappointed with these numbers. Nine thousand full-time jobs at this stage of the cycle...is nothing to write home about."
IVAN COLHOUN, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, BAIN AND CO:

"Even stripping out the Census workers you have had 28,000 growth in the month. This is another strong number among a string of strong numbers recently. We have had strong retail sales, housing finance, and credit and now not a weak employment figure. Most of this data preceeds or is coincident with the last rate cut which the RBA described as a confidence booster. It would seem the chances of another cut are somewhat less than some people are saying. I think this is a bit of a bearish number for the short end."
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA RESEARCH AUSTRALIA:

"It's a fairly strong number. Employment growth it's picking up slowly, its average 12,000 to 13,000 a month in trend terms. It's not making any inroads into the unemployment rate, but you've probably seen the worst of the labour market weakness now. It probably doesn't change the outlook for policy right now and it leaves the question of another easing fairly open."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
